Injurious

in-JOOR-ee-uhs · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Injurious is causing or likely to cause harm or damage.

Long stretches at a poorly adjusted desk proved injurious to the writer's wrists.

Worked Example

The report concluded that the pesticide, while effective against the beetles, was also injurious to the bee population nearby.

The chemical caused real, measurable harm to something beyond its intended target, which is the damage injurious points to.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

harmful: causing or likely to cause harm

damaging: causing damage or harm

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

beneficial: producing good or helpful results

harmless: not able to cause damage or harm

Where it sits · how much damage it does — unhelpful → injurious → devastating

unhelpful vs. injurious: Unhelpful is much weaker than injurious: unhelpful advice simply fails to help, while injurious advice goes further and actually causes real harm or damage.

devastating vs. injurious: Devastating is more severe than injurious: an injurious rumor causes real harm, but a devastating one goes further, leaving overwhelming, sometimes unrecoverable damage behind.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — injury

root — injury: physical harm or damage (from Latin injuria, 'a wrong') (Latin injuria)

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Injurious is injury ('harm or damage') plus -ious, 'full of.' Something injurious is full of the capacity to cause injury.

Use the root in a new word: injury

Use the root in a new word: injury: The gymnast's knee injury from years earlier still ached before every competition.
